content: 1. Pai and Schito (2015) provided a comprehensive overview of the landscape, priorities, needs, and future prospects in tuberculosis diagnostics as of 2015. Their work emphasized the critical gaps in diagnostic tools and the need for innovation to address these challenges. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) released consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment, specifically focusing on drug-resistant TB. These guidelines provide detailed recommendations for managing and treating patients with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). 3. Dowdy et al. (2014) conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of rapid susceptibility testing for second-line TB drugs. Their findings highlighted the economic and clinical benefits of implementing such testing in TB management programs. 4. Van’t Hoog et al. (2015) explored the potential of multiplex high-throughput molecular assays for early detection of drug resistance mutations in TB. Their decision-analytic modeling study demonstrated how these assays could improve infection control and reduce costs. 5. Pantoja, Kik, and Denkinger (2015) examined the costs associated with novel TB diagnostics and questioned whether countries, particularly those with limited resources, could afford these advancements. 6. Padmasawitri et al. (2018) systematically reviewed disparities in model-based cost-effectiveness analyses of TB diagnostics. Their findings underscored the variability in economic evaluations and the need for standardized methodologies. 7. Adepoyibi et al. (2018) identified the most critical attributes within target product profiles (TPPs) for TB diagnostics. Their study emphasized the importance of focusing on specific characteristics to guide the development of effective diagnostic tools. 8. Cocco et al. (2020) conducted a systematic review of current methods for developing TPPs for medical tests. Their work provided insights into the methodologies used to define the desired characteristics of diagnostic tools. 9. Sun et al. (2013) modeled the impact of alternative strategies for rapid molecular diagnosis of TB in Southeast Asia. Their study highlighted the potential benefits of implementing rapid diagnostic technologies in high-burden regions. 10. Nathavitharana et al. (2016) evaluated the performance of two molecular line probe assays, Hain GenoType MTBDRplus version 2 and Nipro NTM+MDRTB, for detecting rifampin and isoniazid resistance. Their multicenter study confirmed the non-inferiority of these assays compared to existing methods. 11. The WHO issued policy guidance on the use of molecular line probe assays for detecting resistance to second-line anti-TB drugs. This document provides recommendations for integrating these assays into TB diagnostic workflows. 12. Helb et al. (2010) demonstrated the utility of on-demand, near-patient technology for the rapid detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampin resistance. Their study highlighted the potential of these technologies to improve TB diagnosis in resource-limited settings. 13. Dalton et al. (2012) investigated the prevalence and risk factors for resistance to second-line drugs in MDR-TB patients across eight countries. Their prospective cohort study provided valuable insights into the global burden of drug-resistant TB. 14. Horne et al. (2013) assessed the diagnostic accuracy and reproducibility of WHO-endorsed phenotypic drug susceptibility testing methods for firstand second-line anti-TB drugs. Their findings supported the reliability of these methods in clinical practice. 15. Claassens et al. (2013) examined the role of health system delays in initiating TB treatment among patients in primary care. Their study highlighted the need for systemic improvements to reduce diagnostic and treatment delays. 16. Sreeramareddy et al. (2009) conducted a systematic review of time delays in diagnosing pulmonary TB. Their findings emphasized the importance of timely diagnosis to improve patient outcomes and reduce transmission. 17. Denkinger et al. (2013) evaluated the readiness of peripheral microscopy centers for next-generation molecular TB diagnostics. Their study identified key challenges and opportunities for implementing advanced diagnostic technologies in resource-limited settings. 18. The WHO developed a quality assurance policy for diagnostic products, emphasizing the importance of maintaining high standards in TB diagnostics to ensure accuracy and reliability. 19. Andre et al. (2016) discussed the connectivity of diagnostic technologies and their role in improving TB surveillance and accelerating elimination efforts. Their work highlighted the potential of digital solutions to enhance diagnostic workflows. 20. Kuupiel et al. (2017) proposed strategies to improve the accessibility and efficiency of point-of-care diagnostic services in lowand middle-income countries. Their study emphasized the importance of lean and agile supply chain management. 21. Parsons et al. (2011) reviewed the challenges and opportunities in laboratory diagnosis of TB in resource-poor countries. Their work underscored the need for innovative solutions to address diagnostic gaps in these settings. 22. The WHO conducted a Delphi-like consultation and public comment process to refine the TPP for a rapid test to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis at the peripheral level. This process involved extensive expert input and consensus-building to define the desired characteristics of the test. 23. The consultation process revealed high levels of agreement on key aspects of the TPP, including target populations, performance characteristics, and operational requirements. However, some areas, such as the use of non-sputum samples and pricing, required further clarification and revision. 24. The group emphasized the importance of rapid, simple, and easy-to-use tests that require clinically relevant and easy-to-collect samples. They also highlighted the need for affordable pricing to ensure accessibility in resource-limited settings. 25. The final TPP incorporated feedback from the consultation process, balancing the need for high performance and operational feasibility with considerations for cost and accessibility.
